Stated Claim / Post Context:
‘Horrified... and not surprised at all’ | Tennessee public defender on Christa Pike’s failed execution

After the state’s second failed execution of Christa Gail Pike, federal public defenders say systemic failures inside the Tennessee Department of Correction were predictable consequences of the state’s lethal injection protocol.

Actual Article Body:
What This Story Is About

Why It Matters

What Happens Next

For Context

Catch Up

KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT) - After the state’s second failed execution of Christa Gail Pike, federal public defenders say systemic failures inside the Tennessee Department of Correction were predictable consequences of the state’s lethal injection protocol.

Pike, 50, was still breathing after two syringes of lethal pentobarbital on Wednesday evening at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville before the execution was called off and she was transported to a local hospital.

She currently remains hospitalized and on a ventilator, according to her lawyer.

The incident follows the attempted execution of death row inmate Tony Carruthers, who suffered a failed execution just five months prior.

In an interview with WVLT News, Kit Thomas, Deputy Chief of the Capital Habeas Unit at the Federal Public Defender’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee, said death row defense attorneys warned state officials about these exact outcomes when TDOC introduced its revised lethal injection protocol in early 2025.

“I’m horrified about what Christa Pike experienced, and I’m not surprised at all,” Thomas said. “These concerns were not just foreseeable, they were foreseen.”

Thomas said that her unit represents people who have been sentenced to death in federal habeas corpus appeals and constitutional challenges to state execution methods. In March 2025, the office sued TDOC on behalf of multiple death row inmates, challenging the legality and medical soundness of the updated procedures.

“There are paragraphs of our lawsuit that have literally come true,” Thomas said. “Our concerns were that someone was going to be strapped to a gurney for a prolonged period of time while these underqualified individuals attempted to establish IV access, and Mr. Carruthers lived out that reality.”

According to Thomas, TDOC’s revised 2025 guidelines lacked in qualifications required for execution personnel who are tasked with finding veins and administering lethal substances to those on death row.

“The revised 2025 protocol under Commissioner Frank Strada’s leadership provides pretty vague standards for who can be hired as an IV team member,” Thomas said. “It’s to the point that I could go take a phlebotomy course over the weekend and technically be qualified to be an IV team member on TDOC’s execution team.”

You can find the entire briefing packet below:

Thomas noted that in Strada’s previous role as the deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections, he oversaw three executions that were also complicated by prolonged struggles to place intravenous lines.

Additionally, Thomas adds that in Strada’s deposition last year, he acknowledged modeling Tennessee’s updated protocol after Arizona procedures, which were regulations Arizona had discarded of following these incidents.

“Frank Strada was hired to clean up a broken lethal injection system in Tennessee, and he brought with him the problems from Arizona,” Thomas said.

On Wednesday night, media witnesses present for the execution said that Pike complained of severe pain, stating her arm felt like it was “about to burst open” and that a section of her arm was “really throbbing” while the lethal injection process was taking place.

From this, Thomas noted two issues as to why the fatal dose failed to end Pike’s life.

“What could have happened was that there was vein extravasation, that the needle punctured the vein and went through the other side,” Thomas said, adding that drug degradation remains another potential issue. “Again, this is all speculation. We need to know more, and hopefully we’ll know more in the coming weeks and months.”
